I’m 61, been at this 3D stuff less than 2 years & my oldest model is less than 15 months old. It’s an excuse to use AI.

You want tough, try designing in Bambu Studio exclusively & working within it’s limitations. I’m hoping the skills I learn within Bambus studio translate into a “real” design software somewhere down the road.

I spent hours on my last creation (Emergency 10mm Socket Holder) figuring out how to place all my “negative” parts within the model so it would “mesh bolean” properly (it doesn’t like 90 degree negative parts apparently) as my angles were “too” sharp. I figured out to to “stack” negative parts upon/next to each other & found a way to make my model work.

I then printed my model (both designs), & once I was happy with the outcome, I uploaded them to Makerworld.

AI is NOT creating

items.title: [LoRaMeshDevices] This Tiny Meshtastic Node Is Solar Ready: Base Uno First Look
items.content_html:
🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

The Muzi Works Base Uno caught my attention because it packs quite a few useful features into a very small Meshtastic board. It comes pre-flashed, includes a 1,500 mAh battery, and has dedicated connections for a solar panel. That is a pretty interesting starting point for a little off-grid node. I bought the kit to find out how easily it would get going and whether the solar input actually worked. By the end of my first round of testing, it had connected over Bluetooth, discovered nearby nodes, completed a traceroute, and charged its battery to around 96% using a small solar panel. So far, this little board is looking good. Key Takeaways The Base Uno kit includes a pre-flashed Meshtastic board, antenna, and 1,500 mAh three-wire LiPo battery. Bluetooth pairing worked with PIN 123456, and I retained Long Fast to match my existing mesh. A small solar panel connected to PV+ and ground raised the reported battery level to about 96%. The app eventually showed 33 online nodes, and a traceroute to a node roughly a mile away succeeded. Table of Contents What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh Node Discovery Took a Little Patience Connecting a Small Solar Panel More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The kit includes the essentials for getting the board powered up and connected: The Base Uno board, carrying Elecrow and Muzi Works branding. A small screw-on antenna. A USB cable. A 1,500 mAh rechargeable LiPo battery. A small Allen key and screws. The board itself is quite compact. There is a reset button and a user button, but no display. Configuration and status checks happen through the Meshtastic app rather than on a screen attached to the node. Its nRF processor is one reason I was interested in it. This is the sort of hardware I would expect to be light on battery use, which makes it appealing for both a portable device and a solar-powered installation. I have not measured its power consumption or battery runtime yet, though, so those remain things to test rather than results from this first look. The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail The included battery stood out more than I expected. It is a 1,500 mAh LiPo with three wires, rather than just the usual positive and negative leads. The third wire is a sensing connection. My understanding is that it provides battery temperature information that the charging circuitry can use to manage charging, including stopping it when conditions are unsuitable. That is particularly interesting on a board intended for solar use. I like seeing that extra sensing connection, but I did not test the temperature cutoff or establish its operating thresholds. The important distinction here is that the battery offers more than a simple two-wire power connection. Confirming exactly how the board responds to that sensing input will need further testing. Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar There is quite a bit available around the edges of this little board: QWIIC port: An expansion connection I plan to try in a separate test. SDA and SCL pins: The labeled I2C connections. TX and RX pins: Serial connections for additional projects. OLED-related connections: Useful options if a display becomes part of the build. PV+ and ground: The dedicated solar-panel connections. Battery connector: Located on the back of the board, separate from the QWIIC port. That last distinction is worth paying attention to during assembly. The battery does not plug into the QWIIC port. I checked the connector location and orientation before seating it in the battery socket on the back. The PV+ and ground connections are what make this especially tempting as a solar-node project. Rather than starting with a separate charging arrangement, there is already a place on the board to bring in the panel. First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Connect the antenna before powering up the node. I screwed on the supplied antenna first, then connected the battery. An LED came on straight away, which was a good start. The package identified the board as pre-flashed with Meshtastic, so there was no initial firmware installation to work through. My setup sequence was straightforward: Attach the antenna. Plug the battery into the correct battery connector. Open the Meshtastic app and look for the node over Bluetooth. Select the discovered Meshtastic device. Enter the Bluetooth pairing PIN. Allow the app to load the node information. Because there is no display, I tried the default PIN, 123456, and it connected successfully. The Bluetooth settings later confirmed that this was the configured PIN. It can be changed there rather than left at the default. My unit arrived running Meshtastic 2.7.15. The app initially reported the battery at 45%, while a later device-metrics reading showed 67%. Those were the reported values during setup, not a controlled battery-capacity measurement. Changing the Node Name I went into the user settings and gave the node a recognizable name using my vervesoft.live naming scheme with a Muzi identifier. Saving the change caused the node to reboot. The Bluetooth connection dropped while it restarted, and the status LED changed colors before the node returned. The same behavior occurred when saving the LoRa settings. A brief disconnect after saving was part of the restart, not a failed setup. Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh The board initially had the Long Fast modem preset selected. My other nodes were still using Long Fast, so I kept this board on the same settings for the first test. Selecting the US region in the app changed the preset to Long Turbo during this setup. I changed it back to Long Fast so the Base Uno would match my existing nodes. These were the US-region combinations shown during the test: Long Fast: Frequency slot 20, operating at 906.875 MHz. Long Turbo: Frequency slot 14, operating at 908.75 MHz. Long Turbo was the newer default I encountered at the time, but compatibility with the mesh I already had running was the immediate priority. There was no point leaving this one node on a different preset while the rest were still waiting to be migrated. Choose the correct region for your location and check that the radio settings match the nodes you intend to use. The US settings above describe this particular setup, not a configuration to copy regardless of country. Other Settings I Checked With the radio configured, I worked through the remaining settings: Channels: A Long Fast channel was already present. Position sharing: The installed firmware allowed it on that channel, with an approximately 1.8-mile position-precision radius shown. Device role: The board was set to Client. Time zone: I used the computer’s time zone. Buzzer: The configuration listed pin 22, although I did not add or test a buzzer. Display: Display settings were turned off. Bluetooth: The fixed PIN was set to 123456. There was no GPS installed on this setup, so the position-sharing option did not mean the board was producing its own GPS location. It also had no environmental readings available. Node Discovery Took a Little Patience At first, the node list stayed empty apart from the Base Uno itself. I enabled the option to include unknown nodes, but there was still nothing else immediately. I expected it to find somebody fairly quickly. Instead of changing everything at once, I left it running and checked a few diagnostics. The signal-quality page did not provide a noise-floor reading with the installed firmware. It did show transmit and receive counters, including one TX and one RX at that stage. Battery telemetry was available, but there was no environmental or position data. Then another node appeared, identified as 49D4. That was the first useful confirmation that the Base Uno was receiving another mesh node. More entries followed as it continued running. The practical lesson from this first startup was simple: an empty node list in the first few minutes did not turn out to mean the board was faulty. In this case, it needed a little time. I also checked the firmware version against the releases available at the time. The unit had 2.7.15, while 2.7.26 was listed as the latest stable release then. I left the firmware alone for this test so I could establish how the kit behaved as supplied. Connecting a Small Solar Panel Once the basic setup was working, I tried the feature that interested me most: solar charging. I took a small panel described as roughly 200 mA and soldered its leads to the PV+ and ground connections on the back of the board. The LiPo battery remained connected, and I placed the assembly outside for a short test. The first solar test used a small panel connected directly to the board’s dedicated solar input. This was a bare-board experiment, not a finished outdoor installation. I still need to find a suitable case before turning it into a permanent node. Solar Charging Results There was a useful amount of sun, followed by some cloud, so the panel did not have uninterrupted sunshine throughout the test. Even so, the reported battery level rose from readings in the 60% to 70% range earlier in the session to approximately 95% to 96%. The device-metrics graph showed the upward charging trend after the assembly had been outside. That is the encouraging result: the solar input worked, and the reported battery charge increased while the node was operating. This was not a measured charging-efficiency test, and it does not yet establish whether this particular panel can sustain the node through nights and poor weather. It does show that the basic solar-charging arrangement is functional. More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute After the board had been running outside for a while, the app showed 33 online nodes with unknown entries filtered out. That was quite a change from the nearly empty list during the first few minutes. I then requested a traceroute to another node, and it returned successfully. The other node was roughly a mile down the road, which was a pleasing result with the little supplied stubby antenna still attached. I would not turn that into a maximum-range claim. This was an initial connectivity check, not a controlled range test. Still, the board was doing the things I wanted to establish first: receiving mesh traffic and completing a traceroute. A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? That is now the interesting decision. The Base Uno is small enough to make a neat portable build, but the dedicated solar input makes a permanent solar node very tempting. For a mobile build, the compact board and included 1,500 mAh battery are appealing. For a solar build, the working panel input and three-wire battery sensing are the details that stand out. My next steps are to find a case, update the firmware, and test the QWIIC port. I also want more time with the power system before making any claims about long-term autonomy. For now, this is a very positive first impression. It booted, paired, accepted configuration changes, discovered nearby nodes, and charged from a small solar panel. That is a pretty good start for a tiny Meshtastic board. Affiliate disclosure: I may earn from qualifying purchases through the product link below. items.title: [Home Assistant] “What the Heck?!” 2026: Everyone at home gets a say
items.content_html:
WHAT THE HECK?! November 2026

TL;DR

All of November is the Month of “What the Heck?!” Tell us what makes Home Assistant hard, confusing, or annoying for you in the WTH category on our forum. Everyone is welcome, and this year we’d love to hear from new and non-technical users, and people living in homes where someone else set it all up. Run Home Assistant yourself? Ask the people you live with how they feel about it!

Let me start with a confession.

I work on Home Assistant all day, for a living. And still, my own home has moments where the people I live with look at me and go: “What the heck?!”

My most recent one? Profile pictures.

For the longest time, your own profile picture in Home Assistant wasn’t actually yours to change. Only an administrator could do it, tucked away in the settings. So if someone in our house wanted a different picture, they had to ask me, every time. For something that is literally your face, that’s a bit odd, isn’t it?

As of Home Assistant 2026.10, every user, administrator or not, can change their own picture straight from their profile. A tiny change, right? Well, my 13-year-old daughter Lilly now changes hers about every week. I’ve officially lost my job as household profile picture administrator. Best demotion ever 😄

Such a small thing, but it made a big difference in how at home she feels in Home Assistant. And that’s the kind of thing we easily overlook when working on it every day.

So, guess what? It’s that time again. For the whole of November, we’re running the Month of “What the Heck?!” 🎉

Wait, what is this again?

We always value your feedback, but don’t often ask for the tough kind outright. That changes this November. For one month, we open the floodgates. No technical words needed, no fancy format. Just one simple question: what in Home Assistant makes you go “what the heck?!”

The setting you can never find. The moment your home did something and nobody in the household had any clue why. The thing you keep missing, and can’t believe isn’t here yet. All those little (and sometimes not so little) frustrations you’ve quietly learned to live with.

We want to hear them. All of them.

We only do this once every two years, and that’s on purpose. Two years is long enough for a lot to change, in Home Assistant itself and the smart home world around it. The technology moves on, and so do our expectations of what a smart home should do. What bugged you last time might be long gone, and something new might be driving you nuts today.

Why we are doing this

This year, the Open Home Foundation has been focusing on making Home Assistant more approachable. In other words: Home Assistant should not only work for the person who set it up. It should work for everyone who lives in the home.

We’ve made good progress so far. But let’s be real: the people building Home Assistant are pretty bad at spotting what’s confusing about Home Assistant. We know where everything is. We know the workarounds. We stopped being confused years ago.

That makes us terrible test subjects. You, on the other hand, are perfect. And so is everyone in your home.

So this is your month. Complain (nicely), discuss, dream out loud, and tell us what would make Home Assistant better for you.

This year, we want to hear from everyone

Previous editions of WTH month were great. But most of what we heard came from a very specific group: the tinkerers. The people who write YAML for fun, run a dozen apps, and know what an entity ID is.

I’m one of you. We are lovely people. Please keep the WTHs coming 😄

But this year, I want to explicitly invite everybody else too.

  • You just started with Home Assistant. Everything is still fresh, and that “huh?” feeling you had during setup is gold to us. Write it down before you get used to it!
  • You don’t consider yourself a “technical” person. You use Home Assistant, but you don’t want to tinker with it. You want things to just work. Tell us where it doesn’t feel that way.
  • You live in a home where someone else runs Home Assistant. Your partner, parent, room-mate, or child set it all up, and now you live with it, every day. Do you ever feel a little locked out of your own home? This is the group we hear from least, and probably the one we can learn the most from. Home Assistant runs entire households, and most people in those households never open a settings page.

Homework for those of us who run Home Assistant at home

If you’re the one who maintains Home Assistant in your household, I have a small favor to ask.

Go ask the people you live with how they feel about it.

Not “is it working?” because they’ll politely say yes. Ask them for real. Fair warning: you might not like all the answers. I certainly didn’t. But there’s so much to learn from that conversation. Some questions to get it going:

  • What’s the one thing about using Home Assistant that annoys you most?
  • Can you find what you need in the app or on the dashboard? Where do you get lost?
  • When Home Assistant does something unexpected, do you understand why? And what do you do about it? (Is the answer “call you”? Yeah, thought so.)
  • Is there something you’d like to do or change in Home Assistant yourself, but you don’t know how (or don’t dare to)?
  • If you could change one thing about Home Assistant, what would it be?

Then bring what you hear to the forum. Even better: help them post it themselves, in their own words. Their words are exactly what we need.

How it works

All WTHs go into the Month of “What the Heck?!” category on our community forum. To keep things useful (and fun) for everyone, a few simple guidelines:

  • Search first, then vote. Someone may have beaten you to it. Give their topic a vote – it tells us how common a problem is – and add your own story in a reply. Every story adds context.
  • One WTH per topic. That makes it possible to discuss, vote on, and track each one.
  • Describe the moment, not the solution. Tell us what happened, what you expected, and why it bugged you. You don’t need to know how to fix it, and you don’t need any technical words. “I wanted to turn off the kitchen lights and couldn’t figure out where they were in the app” is a perfect WTH.
  • Be kind. We are all here because we care about Home Assistant, our homes, and the people in them. That includes the people working on Home Assistant, many of whom are volunteers, doing this in their spare time.

The category is open for the whole of November.

What happens next?

We read all the WTHs. Yes, really.

In past editions, contributors picked up WTHs and fixed them while the month was still running. I would love to see that happen again. If you’re a contributor and spot one you can tackle: go for it!

Beyond the quick fixes, everything you share helps us understand where Home Assistant needs to go next. It shapes how we make Home Assistant approachable for everyone, not just the person holding the admin account.

So, what the heck?!

Whether you’ve been running Home Assistant since the early days, installed it last week, or simply live with someone who won’t stop talking about it: this month is for you.

Tell us what makes Home Assistant hard, what makes you sigh, or what it’s like to live with it.

Head over to the forum and share your WTH!

I’m looking forward to reading every single one of them (well… at least I’ll do my very best 😅).

../Frenck

FAQ

Do I need an account to post?

Yes, you need a free account on our community forum. Signing up only takes a minute.

I have multiple things! Should I put them all in a single topic?

No, please create a separate topic for each one. There is no limit on how many WTH topics you can create. Smaller topics are much easier to discuss, vote on, and pick up.

I don’t run Home Assistant myself, someone else in my home does. Can I still post?

Yes, please! You are exactly who we’d love to hear from this year. You don’t need to know how it all works behind the scenes; just tell us what it’s like to live with it.

I’m posting on behalf of someone in my home. Is that OK?

Absolutely. Just mention that it comes from them, and use their words as much as you can. How they describe it tells us a lot.

English isn’t my first language. Can I still join?

Of course! The forum is in English, but don’t let that stop you. Feel free to use AI or a translation tool to translate your WTH. If you do, please say so in your post, and add your original text in a hidden details block below it, like this:

[details="Original text"]
Your text in your own language.
[/details]

That way, nothing gets lost in translation, and people can always check what you originally meant. This is the same approach we use in our AI policy.

Does it have to be about Home Assistant itself? What about the mobile Companion app, the documentation, or the website?

All of it counts. If it’s part of your Home Assistant experience, it’s a valid WTH.

My WTH from the last edition still isn’t solved. Can I post it again?

Yes! This is a new edition, and a lot has changed since then. Please create a new WTH, and feel free to link to the old one.

Is everything that is reported going to be fixed?

No, there is no guarantee for that. The goal is to make it easy to tell us what bugs you, for one whole month. What you share helps us understand where Home Assistant is hard, and helps shape what we work on next.

My WTH is one of the top-voted ones, so it’s going to be fixed, right?

This is not a popularity contest. Votes help us see how many people run into the same thing, but they don’t guarantee anything gets picked up.

I really want a new integration or app, so I can use my devices. Is this the right place?

No, this event is not for requesting new integrations or apps. Please open a feature request on GitHub for that.

I found a bug, and I’m comfortable with GitHub. Where should I report it?

If you are comfortable using GitHub, please file an issue there instead. That way, it ends up directly with the people who can fix it, and we can track its progress too.

I’m a contributor and want to fix a WTH. How do I let people know?

Awesome! Reply in the WTH topic and link to your pull request. That way, everyone following the topic knows something is happening.

items.title: [Atlas Obscura] Hazelnut Inn in Chilliwack, British Columbia
items.content_html:
In the rural village of Yarrow BC, a three-suite hotel contains a little castle with a moat, a sailing ship wedged into a tower, and an underground house beneath an artificial hillside.

The Hazelnut Inn was built over nine years by the Imagination Corporation, a theme-park design and fabrication company. Its founders, Peter and Hailey Sawatzky, stayed in a restored Roman villa on their honeymoon and wondered why they couldn't build a small castle hotel of their own in Canada.

The Copper Crown Suite, the last to be completed, is a miniature castle. A steel dragon guards its garden gate, and a bridge crosses a tiny moat into the courtyard. Four armoured statues watch over the great hall, and dragons are carved throughout the masonry and woodwork. A secret door leads to a tiny library.

The North Star Suite is built around the stern of the Avellana, a tall ship fabricated in the company's workshop. The ship was craned into position above the garden entrance before the building was framed around it. Inside, mermaids flank the bed, while a hand-painted astrological map covers the domed ceiling of the tower.

The Under Hill Suite is cut into an artificial hillside. Concrete tree roots cross the ceiling, carved rabbit doors open onto the garden, and owl heads are sculpted into the bedposts. Flowers hang to dry in the kitchenette. It looks like the sort of house you might find after taking a wrong turn in a fairytale.

Together, the three suites make the hotel feel like a collection of miniature worlds with beds in them.
